title: Volume 3 — Code hardening beyond flattening
status: Complete teaching draft. Crash-course exercises on hardening techniques beyond control-flow flattening, through concrete LLVM examples. Write and run the examples after finishing the Volume 2 implementation.

home.headline:
One technique.
A whole toolkit.
home.intro: MiniShield flattens control flow — one hardening technique among many. The Volume 1 capstone showed the plugin is a framework that hosts techniques as named passes. This crash course fills it: control-flow integrity, stack canaries, OLLVM-style obfuscation, position independence, and the fuzzing that proves each one still behaves.

aside.label: Roadmap
aside.text: Volume 3 is a crash course, not a second implementation: each technique gets its threat, its mechanism, concrete LLVM IR, and its cost. The OLLVM family you implement in the same plugin; CFI, canaries, and PIE are read and verified with the toolchain.

lessons.title: The code-hardening landscape
lessons.summary: Place control-flow flattening in the threat model, name the hardening families this volume covers, and set the standard for claiming a hardening technique works.
lessons.takeaway: Flattening is one family — obfuscation. Each technique answers a different threat at a different cost, and obfuscation is the only family whose value the final optimizer can remove.

blocks.text: So far MiniShield has implemented one code-hardening technique: control-flow flattening, which rewrites the control flow of an accepted function through a state-machine dispatcher. The final lesson of Volume 1 zoomed out from there: the plugin’s seams — the named-pass registry, per-technique eligibility guard, shared CFG analysis, and the differential and stats harness — are technique-agnostic, so each hardening technique becomes one more named pass. This volume fills that framework with concrete techniques, organized by the threat each one answers rather than by the seam it plugs into. Every chapter follows the same shape: the threat, the mechanism, concrete LLVM IR from the 23.1.5 toolchain, an exercise, and the cost.
Threats and the families that answer them

rows: Reads or patches the program’s logic
Control-flow flattening (Volume 2) · bogus control flow · string encryption · subroutine splitting
Redirects control through a corrupted indirect call, vtable pointer, or function pointer
Corrupts the saved return address and hijacks a function’s return
Predicts where code sits in memory and defeats ASLR
Finds the memory bugs the rest assume are absent
Sanitizers — used in this volume’s tests and fuzzing, not shipped

blocks.text: The table is a division of labor, not a ranking. CFI stops a corrupted vtable pointer from dispatching to the wrong type, but it does nothing against an attacker who simply reads the binary to find the hole. Obfuscation makes that reading harder, but it does not make a buffer overflow safe. A hardening program layers the families so that no single compromise gives the attacker what they need; this volume teaches each layer separately so you can see where the seams are.
Where MiniShield’s flattening sits

Flattening is the obfuscation family’s member in this book. It raises the cost of understanding and changing control flow, and it pays for that at runtime — a state slot, a load, a switch, and the straight-line optimizations the dispatcher destroys — and at the end of the pipeline: a sufficiently aggressive final optimizer can simplify the state machine back toward the original program, and Volume 2’s exit evidence ends with exactly that observation. Obfuscation has a quality problem the other families do not: its value is what survives optimization, not what the pass emits. Every chapter in this volume returns to that question for its technique.
How this volume works

items: Each technique gets the same shape: the threat it answers, the mechanism, concrete LLVM IR generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, a hands-on exercise, and the cost and limits.

The OLLVM family — bogus control flow, string encryption, subroutine splitting — you implement as new passes in the MiniShield plugin, using the capstone recipe (register, guard, builder, orchestrator, fixtures), and you prove each one preserves behavior with the differential-testing method from the Volume 2 testing chapters.
CFI, stack canaries, and position independence are taught by reading and verifying what clang already generates — a from-scratch CFI pass is beyond crash-course scope.
The final lesson fuzzes one of your own passes, because a differential test over a fixed seed covers less than a fuzzer over the same property.

blocks.text: Two terms before the chapters. A threat model is the explicit statement of which attacker you are defending against and what success means for them. Hardening quality is judged on what that attacker can still do after the technique, at what cost to legitimate users — structural observations like “the block count doubled” or “a canary is present” are not quality claims by themselves.

Checkpoint: MiniShield’s flattening raises the cost of reverse engineering. Of the threats in the table, which does it actually answer, which does it leave open, and why is its failure mode different from the failure modes of CFI and canaries?

items: It answers the first row — reading or patching the program’s logic: the flattened CFG hides the control structure behind a dispatcher and a state slot, so understanding or modifying behavior requires modeling the state machine.

It leaves the other rows open: a corrupted indirect call or vtable pointer (the CFI threat), a corrupted return address (the canary threat), and the memory bugs themselves all still work against the flattened program, because flattening rearranges control flow instead of changing what the program executes or where its data lives.

Its failure mode is optimization, not bypass: the final optimizer can prove the state machine’s behavior and simplify it back toward the original CFG (the Volume 2 exit evidence reduces the whole dispatcher to one select), so the shipped artifact can be structurally unhardened. CFI checks and canaries change what the program does at runtime, so they survive optimization; obfuscation’s quality must be judged on the final artifact, not on the pass output.

lessons.title: The indirect call check
lessons.summary: Forward CFI guards indirect calls: read the llvm.type.test + llvm.ubsantrap IR that clang 23.1.5 emits under -fsanitize=cfi-icall -flto, understand why the guard exists only where LTO cannot resolve the target, and verify at runtime that a wrong-type call aborts with SIGILL.
lessons.takeaway: CFI-ICALL is a type test on the callee pointer, inserted by LTO only where the target is genuinely unknown: it aborts wrong-type targets with SIGILL and says nothing about a wrong function of the right type.

blocks.text: Forward CFI (CFI-ICALL) answers the first concrete threat in the landscape: an attacker overwrites a function pointer — via a buffer overflow, a corrupted pointer table, a data race — and the program calls whatever the pointer now says. The pointer is data, and the call site trusts it unconditionally. Forward CFI inserts a guard before every indirect call: verify that the target has the expected function type before dispatching. In LLVM 23.1.5 the guard is the `llvm.type.test` intrinsic paired with `llvm.ubsantrap`, not the legacy `llvm.cfi_icheck` intrinsic that older material describes.
The check in IR

Minimal case: a program obtains a function pointer from an extern function — outside this translation unit, so the compiler can never know where it points. This is what clang 23.1.5 emits with `-fsanitize=cfi-icall -flto -O2` (trimmed from the real capture; `opt -passes=verify` accepts it):

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare ptr @lookup(i32)

declare i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr, metadata)
declare void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 immarg)

define i32 @run_op(i32 %id, i32 %x) {
  %fp = tail call ptr @lookup(i32 %id)
  %ok = tail call i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr %fp, metadata !"_ZTSFiiE")
  br i1 %ok, label %do_call, label %trap

trap:
  tail call void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 2)
  unreachable

do_call:
  %r = tail call i32 %fp(i32 %x)
  ret i32 %r
}

Read it top to bottom. `%fp` is the attacker-controlled pointer: it comes from `lookup`, which lives in another translation unit, so even full LTO cannot resolve it. `%ok` is the guard: `llvm.type.test` asks whether the memory at `%fp` carries a CFI type descriptor matching `_ZTSFiiE` — the mangled type-info name of the function type `int(int)`. The descriptor is attached by the compiler to every function compiled with CFI; a target without one, or with a different one, fails the test. The branch then goes to `do_call`, where the real indirect call happens, or to `trap`, where `llvm.ubsantrap` lowers to an undefined instruction and the process dies with SIGILL (exit 132).

Two things this is not. First, it is not an address check: nothing compares `%fp` against a list of allowed addresses, so a target of the right type but the wrong function still passes. Second, the guard exists only where the target is unknown. Without the flag, the same source compiles to an unconditional indirect call:

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare ptr @lookup(i32)

define i32 @run_op(i32 %id, i32 %x) {
  %fp = tail call ptr @lookup(i32 %id)
  %r = tail call i32 %fp(i32 %x)
  ret i32 %r
}
Where LTO can see the target, the check changes shape

CFI-ICALL is an LTO feature — the flag refuses to work without `-flto`. LTO's job is to resolve indirect calls, so most guards the front end would emit disappear at link time: when the target is provably unique the call is devirtualized or inlined, and there is nothing to guard. Where the target set is small but not fully resolvable, the generic type test degenerates into a comparison against known addresses. In the single-translation-unit demo below, LTO rewrote the guard as:

The parsed address is compared against `0x201830` — the address of `op_right`, the only target of the right type — and a mismatch jumps to the `ud1` trap. Note that `op_right` itself is now a one-instruction thunk that jumps to `op_right.cfi`, the body LTO rebuilt with its CFI type descriptor attached. The shape to take away: the guard appears exactly where the pointer is genuinely unknown at link time — external, data-dependent, attacker-writable — in whatever form is cheapest there.
Proof at runtime

The demo program reads a pointer address from standard input and calls through it; a `self` flag prints the addresses of the two candidate targets (a legal `int(int)` function and a wrong-type `int()` function). It is linked with `-no-pie` so the printed addresses are stable across runs — under ASLR each launch would print different ones (the PIE chapter returns to exactly that point).

$ clang-23 -fsanitize=cfi-icall -flto -O2 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld cfi_pipe.c -o cfi_pipe
$ clang-23 -flto -O2 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld cfi_pipe.c -o cfi_pipe_nocfi
$ ./cfi_pipe self
0x201830 0x201790
$ echo 0x201830 | ./cfi_pipe
result -> 42
$ echo 0x201790 | ./cfi_pipe
Illegal instruction (core dumped)
$ ./cfi_pipe_nocfi self
0x201778 0x201780
$ echo 0x201780 | ./cfi_pipe_nocfi
result -> 99

The legal target dispatches and returns 42. The wrong-type target dies with an illegal instruction — that is the CFI trap, a hard abort, not a report. And in the binary built without CFI, the same wrong-type input does not crash at all: the call goes through, `op_wrong` returns 99, and the program prints it as a normal result. That silent success is the threat CFI removes — a corrupted pointer that lands on a function with a matching calling convention but the wrong behavior; the only observable difference is the wrong answer. CFI turns that into a visible abort.

items: `-fsanitize=cfi-icall` works only with `-flto`, and every object in the link must be CFI-instrumented: a non-CFI target has no type descriptor to match, so even a legal call aborts.

LTO removes every guard whose target it can resolve and folds the rest to the cheapest correct form; a program whose indirect calls all have known targets contains no CFI checks at all, and that is not a misconfiguration.
The check is on the target's type, not its address: a wrong function of the matching signature is still a legal target.
`llvm.ubsantrap` lowers to an undefined instruction (SIGILL, exit 132), not a message; without a debugger the failure looks like a random illegal instruction, not a CFI violation.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: In the demo the wrong-type target aborts and the legal target completes. (a) What does the guard test, and where does the value it matches come from? (b) Why does the guard appear in this program at all? (c) Why is the no-CFI run a more dangerous failure than the CFI run?

items: (a) It tests the target's function-type descriptor: `llvm.type.test` compares what the compiler attached to each CFI-compiled function definition against `_ZTSFiiE`, the mangled type-info name of the function type `int(int)`. It is not an address — a wrong function of the right type still passes.

(b) Because the callee pointer is genuinely unknown at link time: in the minimal module it comes from the extern `lookup`, and in the demo it is parsed from standard input at runtime. LTO can only remove or fold the guard when it can resolve the target, and it cannot here.

(c) Without CFI the wrong-type call silently succeeds — it prints `result -> 99` and exits 0: the corruption achieved its goal and nobody knows. With CFI the process aborts with SIGILL: the hijack is blocked and visible. A check that fails silently is worse than no check, because it hides the attack; CFI's value is in making the failure a crash.

lessons.title: The vtable check
lessons.summary: Backward CFI guards virtual calls: read the vtable-pointer llvm.type.test that clang++ 23.1.5 emits under -fsanitize=cfi-vcall, understand which corruptions it catches and which it misses, and verify at runtime that a wrong-class vtable aborts while a derived-class vtable passes.
lessons.takeaway: CFI-VCALL tests the vtable pointer against the static base-class descriptor before dispatch: it catches an object with the wrong class's vtable, not a legitimate vtable with corrupted slots.

blocks.text: CFI-ICALL guards the callee pointer. The more common C++ threat is one level up: the object's vtable pointer. A corrupted vptr — a type-confusion write, a buffer overflow that reaches the first word of an object, a stale pointer into a reused allocation — makes `b->apply(x)` dispatch to a completely unrelated class. CFI-VCALL inserts a guard before every virtual call: the vtable pointer must point into the type-info hierarchy of the call site's static base class.
The check is on the vtable pointer

Captured with clang++ 23.1.5 and `-fsanitize=cfi-vcall -fvisibility=hidden -flto -O2` (hidden visibility is required; the flag is refused without it). Trimmed from the real capture, `opt -passes=verify` accepts it:

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr, metadata)
declare void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 immarg)

define i32 @run_op(i64 %obj, i32 %x) {
  %objptr = inttoptr i64 %obj to ptr
  %vtable = load ptr, ptr %objptr, align 8
  %ok = call i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr %vtable, metadata !"_ZTS4Base")
  br i1 %ok, label %do_call, label %trap

trap:
  call void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 2)
  unreachable

do_call:
  %slot = load ptr, ptr %vtable, align 8
  %r = call i32 %slot(ptr %objptr, i32 %x)
  ret i32 %r
}

Two differences from the ICALL guard. The pointer under test is not a function address but the vtable pointer loaded from the object's first word — `%vtable = load ptr, ptr %objptr`. And the descriptor is not a function-type name but the mangled class name of the call site's static type: `_ZTS4Base` is the type-info name of `Base`. `llvm.type.test` succeeds when the vtable belongs to `Base` or to a class derived from it — C++'s dynamic-type rule, enforced at every dispatch. If it passes, dispatch proceeds exactly as usual: load slot 0 of the vtable and call through it.

Together the pair covers the two indirect dispatches a C++ program performs: ICALL tests a function pointer against the function's type; VCALL tests a vtable pointer against the class's type. Same intrinsic, same trap, different operand and different descriptor.
Proof at runtime

$ clang++-23 -fsanitize=cfi-vcall -fvisibility=hidden -flto -O2 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld vcall_pipe.cpp -o vcall_pipe
$ ./vcall_pipe self
0x203df8 0x203e00
$ echo 0x203df8 | ./vcall_pipe
result -> 42
$ echo 0x203e00 | ./vcall_pipe
Illegal instruction (core dumped)

The program prints the addresses of two static objects — a `Derived` (which derives from `Base`) and an `Evil` (which does not) — and then dispatches through the address read from standard input. `Derived` passes: its vtable is in `Base`'s hierarchy, and the call returns 42. `Evil` fails: it does not derive from `Base`, so its vtable is not registered under `Base`'s type-info, and the type test aborts the process before any vtable slot is loaded.

The boundary matters. CFI-VCALL catches the vtable being the wrong class, not the right class with the wrong slots: an attacker who overwrites slot 0 of a legitimate `Derived` vtable to point at their own function still passes the check, because the vtable pointer is in the right hierarchy, and the hijack goes through. That is the same type-versus-address distinction as the previous lesson, one level up.

items: `-fsanitize=cfi-vcall` requires `-fvisibility=hidden`; the compiler rejects the flag without it.
The check is on the vtable pointer (the object's first word), not on the method pointer loaded from the vtable: a corrupted slot in a legitimate class's vtable is not caught.
Like CFI-ICALL this is an LTO feature: calls LTO can devirtualize — the common case once it has proved the dynamic type — carry no guard at all.

The descriptor is the static type at the call site (here `Base`); a call through a pointer of a more-derived type is checked against that more-derived type, so the check composes up the derivation chain.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: In the demo the `Derived` dispatch succeeds and the `Evil` dispatch aborts. (a) Which pointer does the guard test, and against which descriptor? (b) Why does clang require `-fvisibility=hidden` for this flag? (c) What corruption of a legitimate vtable would this check not stop?

items: (a) The vtable pointer loaded from the object's first word, tested against `_ZTS4Base` — the type-info name of the call site's static base class — not against the address of the method that will be called.

(b) The guard compares the object's vtable pointer against a local, compile-time-known vtable/type-info address. With default-visibility type-info symbols the dynamic linker can interpose a different copy from another shared object, and the check would silently test against the wrong address; `-fvisibility=hidden` pins the type-info symbols to the local copies, which is why clang accepts the flag only with it.

(c) A corrupted slot inside a legitimate vtable: overwrite slot 0 of a real `Derived` vtable to point at attacker code and the vtable pointer still points into the right hierarchy, the check passes, and the dispatch is hijacked. CFI-VCALL verifies which class an object claims to be, not what that class's vtable points to.

lessons.title: The stack canary check
lessons.summary: Read the stack canary the way clang 23.1.5 actually emits it: the sspstrong attribute in the IR, the TLS plant/compare/abort machinery in the machine code, which functions each -fstack-protector mode protects, and the runtime proof that the same overflow is a silent hijack without the canary and a visible abort with it.
lessons.takeaway: A stack canary is a per-process random value planted between the buffer and the saved return address and checked at function exit: it turns the classic return-address hijack into a visible abort, but it only guards what its own frame guards — not globals, not the heap, not unprotected functions, and not a leaked guard.

blocks.text: Stack canaries answer the control-data row of the threat table: an attacker overwrites the saved return address of a function — the classic buffer overflow — and the function returns into their code instead of its caller. The canary is a random value planted in the frame between the vulnerable buffer and the saved return address, and compared on the way out: if the overflow reached the return address, it crossed the canary, and the comparison aborts the process before the corrupted return executes. Unlike CFI, the canary changes what data the frame holds rather than what the control flow may target.
One thing to hold in mind while reading this chapter: you will not find the canary in the IR. This is what clang 23.1.5 actually leaves behind, and where the check really lives.
The canary is not in the IR

The vulnerable function is `process`, an unchecked copy of an attacker-controlled length into a 16-byte buffer. Compiled with `-fstack-protector-strong -O0`, the module is (attribute bundle trimmed; `opt -passes=verify` accepts it):

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i64 @strlen(ptr noundef)
declare void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr noalias writeonly, ptr noalias readonly, i64, i1 immarg)

; clang 23.1.5, -fstack-protector-strong -O0; attribute bundle trimmed
define dso_local i32 @process(ptr noundef %line) #0 {
  %2 = alloca ptr, align 8
  %3 = alloca [16 x i8], align 16
  %4 = alloca i32, align 4
  store ptr %line, ptr %2, align 8
  store i32 0, ptr %4, align 4
  %5 = getelementptr inbounds [16 x i8], ptr %3, i64 0, i64 0
  %6 = load ptr, ptr %2, align 8
  %8 = call i64 @strlen(ptr noundef %6)
  call void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr align 16 %5, ptr align 1 %6, i64 %8, i1 false)
  %9 = load i32, ptr %4, align 4
  %10 = add nsw i32 %9, 1
  ret i32 %10
}

attributes #0 = { sspstrong "stack-protector-buffer-size"="8" }

Grep this module for a canary and you find nothing: no intrinsic, no call, no store. The entire trace of the protection in the IR is `sspstrong` in the function's attribute bundle, alongside the `"stack-protector-buffer-size"` value. The default build of the same source is identical except that `sspstrong` is absent from the bundle — no other IR byte changes. (LLVM 23 does define an `llvm.stackprotector` intrinsic in its Intrinsics.td — it "writes the stack guard to the correct place on the stack frame" — but this C pipeline never emits it; the guard is materialized directly in machine code.) The backend, reading the attribute, is what generates the canary.
The machine code where the canary lives

This is the backend's output for the same function (`-fstack-protector-strong -O0`; `.cfi` directives omitted). The frame is `subq $64`: the buffer at `-32(%rbp)`, the canary slot at `-8(%rbp)`, the saved return address at `+8(%rbp)`:

process:
	pushq	%rbp
	movq	%rsp, %rbp
	subq	$64, %rsp
	movq	%fs:40, %rax
	movq	%rax, -8(%rbp)
	movq	%rdi, -40(%rbp)
	movl	$0, -44(%rbp)
	movq	-40(%rbp), %rdi
	movq	%rdi, -56(%rbp)
	callq	strlen@PLT
	movq	-56(%rbp), %rsi
	movq	%rax, %rdx
	leaq	-32(%rbp), %rdi
	callq	memcpy@PLT
	movl	-44(%rbp), %eax
	incl	%eax
	movl	%eax, -48(%rbp)
	movq	%fs:40, %rax
	movq	-8(%rbp), %rcx
	cmpq	%rcx, %rax
	jne	.LBB1_2
	movl	-48(%rbp), %eax
	addq	$64, %rsp
	popq	%rbp
	retq
.LBB1_2:
	callq	__stack_chk_fail@PLT

Read it in three beats. Entry: `movq %fs:40, %rax` loads the guard from per-process TLS, and `movq %rax, -8(%rbp)` plants the copy in the frame between the buffer and the return address — exactly the placement the `--help` text promises: the guard "must be positioned in the stack frame such that a buffer overflow from a vulnerable variable will overwrite the guard value before overwriting the function's return address." Exit: the guard is reloaded from TLS, compared with the planted copy, and a mismatch jumps to `callq __stack_chk_fail@PLT`, which aborts the process. Note the value's origin: one random number in TLS per process — the same value is planted in every protected frame, not one per frame.
Which functions get a canary
The mode flag selects which frames the backend protects. Three function shapes in one TU, compiled four ways (clang 23.1.5, `-O0`):

rows: takes the address of a local

blocks.text: The `--help` text states the heuristics: plain mode protects functions with char arrays larger than 8 bytes; strong adds arrays of any type, `alloca` calls, and taking the address of a local variable; `-all` protects every function. Note that `f_ptr` trips strong because of `memcpy(&c, ...)` — the address of a local — not because of its pointer parameter. And the default of this toolchain is no canaries at all: many distributions' compilers turn on `-fstack-protector-strong` by default, but the conda clang here does not, which is why every command in this lesson spells the flag out.
Proof at runtime

The demo builds a 56-byte payload in `main` — 24 bytes of padding, then the address of `sink` (a function that prints and exits) repeated four times — and passes it to `process` with its explicit length, so no NUL byte in the address can truncate the copy. The spray covers whichever 8-byte slot the saved return address lands in. As in the CFI chapter, `-no-pie` keeps the printed addresses stable across runs.

$ clang-23 -O0 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld canary_pipe.c -o canary
$ clang-23 -fstack-protector-strong -O0 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld canary_pipe.c -o canary_strong
$ ./canary self
0x201810
$ echo 0x201810 | ./canary
HACKED: process returned into sink
$ echo 0x201810 | ./canary_strong
*** stack smashing detected ***: terminated
Aborted (core dumped)

Without the canary, the overflow rewrites the saved return address to `sink`: the program prints `HACKED` and the hijack has succeeded silently — exit 0, no error of any kind. With the canary, the same overflow smashes the guard at `-8(%rbp)` on its way to the return address; the exit check finds the mismatch and aborts before the corrupted return executes — exit 134 (SIGABRT), "stack smashing detected." Same overflow, same payload: one build lets the attack land, the other turns it into a crash. That is the canary's value proposition, and it is the same shape as CFI's — a silent compromise becomes a visible abort — aimed at control data instead of control-flow targets.
What the canary does not stop

items: Global or heap function pointers: the canary guards the saved return address of one frame. It says nothing about a corrupted pointer in `.data` or on the heap, which never touches the frame.
Functions the heuristic did not protect: `f_math` above carries no guard and no check, so an overflow in an unprotected frame is invisible to the canary.
Corrupted locals used before the return: if an overflow stops short of the guard slot — say, clobbering a vtable pointer in a local object — the damage is done while the canary is still intact.
A known guard: the value is one random number per process, in TLS. An attacker who can read memory can read the canary and write it back around the overflow.

Buffers the final optimizer erases: at `-O2`, `process` becomes `movl $1, %eax; retq` — the buffer, the overflow, and the canary all disappear together, because the protection only survives as long as the state it protects does.

blocks.text: The cost is small and local: one TLS load at entry, one store, one TLS load plus one compare at exit, per protected function, plus a cold branch to the abort. It is a runtime check in the same class as the CFI trap, not a compile-time property — and like the CFI trap, its whole value is in aborting loudly rather than continuing wrong.

items: The canary lives in machine code, not IR: grepping the `.ll` for a guard finds nothing. The evidence is the `sspstrong` attribute in the bundle and the `%fs:` load in the asm.
The guard is per-process, not per-frame: one TLS value for the whole address space. Leaking that one value defeats every canary in the process.
The demo is `-O0` on purpose: at `-O2` the optimizer erases the vulnerable buffer and the protection disappears with the state it protects.
Partial corruption of the guard slot is enough to trip the check: the compare covers all 8 bytes, so any overlap of the overflow with the guard aborts.
This toolchain's default is no canaries; the flag is explicit in every command in this lesson.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: In the demo the no-canary build reaches `sink` and the canary build aborts. (a) Where does the guard value come from, and where in the frame is it planted? (b) What is the only trace of the protection in the IR, and why does that make the canary invisible to an IR-only reader? (c) Name one overflow that still succeeds against the canary build, and say why the canary cannot see it.

items: (a) The guard is a per-process value in TLS (`movq %fs:40, %rax` — the same number for every frame in the process). Entry stores a copy in the frame at `-8(%rbp)`, between the vulnerable buffer at `-32(%rbp)` and the saved return address at `+8(%rbp)`, so an overflow from the buffer must cross the guard to reach the return address.

(b) `sspstrong` in the function's attribute bundle (with `"stack-protector-buffer-size"`). The frontend only records which frames are eligible; the backend materializes the load/store/compare from that attribute, so an IR-only reader sees no canary instructions at all — the protection is a property of the generated machine code, not of the IR.

(c) For example, overwriting a global function pointer: the canary guards only the saved return address of protected frames. A corrupted dispatch pointer in `.data` never touches any frame's guard, the program dispatches through it, and no canary is ever consulted — the check exists only at the exit of instrumented functions, and only for their own return path.
